title: Leo Burnett 1891-1971
titleCn: 广告大师李奥·贝纳传奇一生
articleHtml:
The advertising man who first exploited the power of the visual image

 

A 

Leo Burnett, founder of the multibillion-dollar advertising agency Leo Burnett Worldwide, had a career spanning nearly six decades, and an aptitude for inventing new business strategies. He is widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in the history of advertising. Unlike many of his contemporaries who viewed advertising as a cynical manipulation of consumer weaknesses, Burnett held high expectancy that every employee should be bowed down to the work. But heaven help you if you were lazy in your approach to dealing with one of his clients. However, if you had a well-thought-out idea, even if he didn't like it, he would respect the effort behind it.

 

B 

Burnett's management style was unconventional for its time. He practised the Removal of physical barriers -- famously taking his office door off its hinges to signal applicability. He also rejected the Group Think approach common in other agencies, believing that collective consensus often diluted creative edge. Instead, he relied on an internal role he called The Creative Right Bower, his number one man who could turn even the wildest idea into a viable campaign. Another innovation was that Burnett regularly invited a professor, a writer, or a businessman from a completely different industry to critique the agency's work. The Outside Expert offered blunt, unfiltered opinions, and knowing their work would be judged by someone unfamiliar with advertising's internal politics, Burnett's employees strove much hard to produce outstanding ideas.

 

C 

Before Burnett entered the advertising field in the 1920s, the industry was dominated by what he called 'advertese' --a straightedge style of descriptive words emphasizing advantages of products. Advertisements of that era typically described a car as 'superbly engineered' or a soap as 'unquestionably pure', without any attempt to connect emotionally with the consumer. Burnett rejected this approach entirely.He argued that advertising should tell a story, and that the story should be rooted in the product's fundamental truth.

 

D 

One of the first major demonstrations of this philosophy was Burnett's 1942campaign for the American Meat Institute. While other agencies proposed slogans about nutrition Burnett's team produced an advertisement that drew attention to the inherent drama of meat itself which was hardly seen in other ads. The now-famous visual show sizzling steak, with the simple headline What's on the fire?' The campaign did not mention vitamins or proteins. Instead, it appealed directly to the senses - the sound, the smell, the anticipation. This approach was considered highly original because it avoided product feature listing and instead dramatised the product in use.

 

E 

Perhaps Burnett's most celebrated achievement was his work for Marlboro cigarettes. In the early 1950s, Marlboro was positioned as a woman`s cigarette,with a red filter tip to hide lipstick marks. Sales were stagnant. Burnett's agency took over the account and faced a seemingly impossible task how to rebrand a “ladies' cigarette” for a broader market. The solution became advertising legend. Burnett and his team created the Marlboro Man-a cowboy figure that symbolised masculinity. independence and the open West. What made this campaign truly significant was that it appealed to a t segment that not previously bought the product. By deliberately shifting away from female smokers and aiming at working-class men, Burnett transformed Marlboro into the world's best-selling cigarette within a decade. The campaign succeed not by inventing a new product,but by inventing a new identity

 

F 

Throughout his career, Burnett developed a distinctive set of creative principles. He often looked for fundamental concepts that could serve as the foundation of an advertising idea - concepts he called inherent drama' or emotional truth'.were not abstract theories: they were practical tools for finding the core story within any product. He considered creativity as the single most important factor in success. He also aimed to design visuals that would reach the viewer without being consciously processed - images that spoke directly to the subconscious instead of consciousness. Finally. his advertisements were designed to connect with people's most fundamentals, such as the need for belonging or security - what he called consumers` innate instincts. Unlike the hard-sell tactics of his era. Burnett's work invited the consumer to participate in a story.

 

G 

Decades after his death in 1971, Burnett's legacy remains remarkably intact. Some of his advertising characters, such as the Jolly Green Giant or Tony the Tiger,now appear outdated in their visual style. Yet the underlying principles have not aged. Due to today`s consumers have grown more sceptical of hyperbole and resistant to traditional hard sell, Burnett's approach -storytelling, emotional truth and visual immediacy - seems more relevant than ever, Indeed, many contemporary digital marketers explicitly cite Burnett as a precursor to modern content marketing. His original ideas still hold influence advertising today, from the use of authentic narrative the rejection of 'advertese'. And far from becoming less important, the visual aspect of advertising has dramatically since Burnett's era, with social media platforms placing image a the centre of consumer engagement.
